translations.text: Rays illuminate the sons of light, and the messages of light make them radiant. The light of those who worship God is devotion to God, which dispels the haze and fog of ignorance. The light of truth dawns upon those who love learning. Just as this visible light illuminates the body, so truth illuminates the soul. By day we distinguish the sick from the healthy, the beautiful from the ugly, the low from the high, the level from the uneven, the road from the way astray, thorns from vine shoots, and mud from springs; but at night, everything in appearance [?]. Likewise, brothers, when truth dawns, it [?] ignorance and reveals the health of faith and the sickness of unbelief, the beauty of humility and the ugliness of excess, the baseness of arrogance and the levelness of uprightness, the willfulness of wickedness, the vine shoots of virtue and the thorns of sins, the mud of desire and the springs of righteous deeds.

For this very reason, blessed David sings of light and truth together in a single song, saying, “Send out your light and your truth.” What light and truth does he wish to have sent? Clearly, it is that light of which John says, “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into the world.” For our Lord Jesus Christ is the true light, the ray of devotion to God, the sun of righteousness, the dawn of truth, which rises from on high and gives light from the earth. From on high, according to the glory of his divinity, he [?]; and from the earth, according to his dispensation in the flesh, he ascends. The dawn, which is the spiritual light, rises from on high, according to blessed Zechariah, the father of John the Forerunner, who says, “Through this the dawn from on high has visited us.” This same dawn also rises from the earth, of which his namesake Zechariah, among the twelve prophets, says, “Behold a man, and his name is Dawn.”

And from where does it rise? David explains: “Truth sprang up from the earth.” What truth? Do not learn from me, but directly from the giver of life to all: “I am,” he says, “the way and the truth and the life.” As was already stated in the first discourse, his nature is simple and extended, indivisible, incorporeal, and without form, as is his Father who begot him. And in his benevolence he takes various names upon himself. He is called the way, to drive away wandering; truth, to destroy falsehood; and life, to abolish death.

And see how often he assumes names that seem contrary in wording but agree in their effects. The same one is a shepherd; the same one is a sheep. “I am,” he says, “the good shepherd.” And how is he a sheep? John says, “Behold the Lamb of God.” Those who wish to introduce distinctions through different names say, “How can a sheep and a shepherd have one nature?” Is Christ’s nature then divided by its various names? It is plainly evident that the various names signify not his essence but his activities. He calls himself a shepherd and is also named a sheep. He is called a priest and is also named the priest’s temple. He is a priest according to the saying, “You are a priest according to the order of Melchizedek”; and a temple according to the saying, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

Let all error be uprooted, and let truth take hold and reign over everyone as king. For our Lord Jesus Christ called himself the vine, as indeed he was, and as we discussed in the assembly, and called the Father the vine grower—not introducing any alteration in his nature, but describing the renewal brought about by his saving work. For everything given to the people of old was ruined. The priesthood was given, and it became corrupt; kingship was given, and prophecy was given. Israel became a [?] vine, as the prophet Jeremiah also says, and instead of the fruit of devotion to God, it produced injustice. Likewise, Isaiah says, ‘I stood waiting for grapes, and it produced thorns.’ And because he saw everything ruined and grown old through negligence, he came and personally renewed everything. He becomes all things to everyone, not by being divided himself, but by arranging everything according to a single plan.

And the Scriptures testify that all this had been ruined and corrupted among the Jews. They say, “Their priests did not say, ‘Where is the Lord?’ Their prophets practiced divination for silver, their apostles did not know me, their rulers dishonored me, and my people did not know me.” And because everything, including the orders of divine worship, had been ruined, he came in person to restore the priesthood, establish the kingship, and renew prophecy; and through his gifts of grace he renews everything that had been ruined and corrupted. The priesthood was ruined, and he himself became a priest. Of him the apostle says, “We have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.” And because the kingship of the Jews had been taken away, the King of the saints came and entered. Of him Nathanael says, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel.” And because false prophecies had obscured prophecy, God withdrew the gift of prophecy because of the unworthiness of the inhabitants of the land. He came again in person to renew prophecy, as the blessed Moses also said: “The Lord God will raise up a prophet for you.”

Thus he was a prophet, a priest, and a king—not because he himself needed that honor, but to raise up what had fallen. For the King of kings had no need of kingship; the one who received service from every priesthood did not lack priesthood; and the one who was the source of prophecy and poured forth streams of righteousness through all the prophets had no need of prophecy. Rather, he came to raise up everything that had fallen, and to restore and renew everything that had been ruined. He also found the vine of Israel corrupted, of which David says, “You brought the vine out of the land of the Egyptians; you uprooted the nations and planted it.” And, renewing what had been corrupted, he says, “I am the true vine.” It is not that he is by nature some created thing; rather, through grace he renews what has been corrupted. If the vine is a created thing, how can he sow like a cultivator of the vine? Speaking of his own teaching, he says, “Behold, the sower went out to sow.” And he himself explains who the sower is: “The one who sows the seed,” he says, “is the Son of Man.” How, then, can one and the same be both a created thing and a cultivator who sows seeds? Unless you distinguish and assign the one to his divinity and the other to his dispensation in the flesh, you confuse these things with one another and will not understand the truth. “I am the vine,” he says, and he calls himself the cultivator of the vine, just as elsewhere he is both shepherd and sheep. From this very point the heretics read badly what was well written, as the prophet also says, “The ways of the Lord are straight, and the righteous will walk in them.” They do not understand what is right, nor what has been clarified and distinguished through the proper ordering of the mind: to assign one part to the honor of his divinity and the other to his governance in the flesh. For this reason they mixed everything together and ruined it, and filled the whole world with the fog of error.

For the Savior, the Lord and lover of humanity, came into this world for our sake. He did not depart from the honor he had before the ages, but adorned it for our sake with his love for humanity. He showed the two bright outlines of the truth: [?] through signs, and his humanity through sufferings. For the one who cannot suffer entered into suffering through what can suffer—not through those passions that lead to sin, but through those that belong to our common nature. For body and spirit are subject to passions that lead to sin, and whoever is free from those passions is also free from sin. This is what is meant: hunger, thirst, weariness, and sleep are bodily needs, but they are not counted as sins. Fornication, impurity, and debauchery, however, which defile the beauty of the body, are sinful passions. The spirit, too, has its own passions, received by nature from the Creator, which are necessary for salvation: fear, sorrow, and anger. If examined on their own, they are called passions, but in moderation and at the proper time they help our nature.

And consider this: there is righteous anger, and wrath called righteous—not anger that flares up without cause, but anger stirred by divine justice, often through the action of the Holy Spirit. It is not when someone becomes angry without cause, but when he is stirred to anger for the sake of devotion to God. Scripture bears witness: ‘The Spirit of the Lord came upon Saul,’ it says, ‘and he became angry.’ When righteous anger is put to use for righteous deeds, Scripture praises it. When it is kindled against impiety, when it serves to silence heretics, when the battle is for the glory of the great King, then showing anger is goodness, and concealing it is treachery. Consider desire too, brother—not the desire that falls into sin, but the desire that orders families through lawful marriage. Consider fear—not fear that is pointless, but fear that is useful and beneficial. For where there is fear of God, there are gifts of goodness; and where there are fears arising from impiety, there are futile deeds. I speak of fear: our Life-giver took upon himself the experiences of body and spirit that are free from sin. In his body he hungered, thirsted, grew weary, and slept. By this he did not dishonor his divinity, but truly revealed the nature of his body. Likewise, in his soul he was afraid, troubled, and sorrowful. ‘My soul is sorrowful to the point of death,’ he says. And again, ‘He began to be sorrowful and troubled.’ These were not sinful experiences, but signs revealing the nature of his body.

And to make it still clearer that such words belong not to his divinity but to his flesh, the life-giver explains to the disciples the nature of his suffering. He says, “My soul is sorrowful to the point of death. Stay awake, so that you do not enter into temptation.” And immediately afterward he says, “My spirit is willing, but my flesh is weak.” Thus he fully and truly reveals the dignity of his divinity and his life in the flesh. He ate as a man; he fed others as one who loves humanity. And what is still more wonderful is that, while he was asking for a drink, he was giving the whole world drink. He says to the Samaritan woman, “Give me a drink.” And he raises his voice and says, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink.” He sleeps on the sea to demonstrate the reality of his bodily nature, and when he rises, he puts the waves of the sea to sleep, so that you may learn that he both sleeps and puts things to sleep. As God, he sees beforehand everything that happens everywhere, and as a man, he travels through the regions of Galilee. And when he comes to stand opposite Bethany, the village of Lazarus, he shows himself both far away and near through the distance between the places. By the power of his divinity he knows everything beforehand. In Galilee he tells of the things happening in Judea. “Lazarus, our friend,” he says, “has fallen asleep”; and he acted in places where he was not present. He comes and stands by the village and says, “Where have you laid him?” And who would dare to bring an accusation of ignorance against Christ because he asked, “Where have you laid him?” And if these words cause you to stumble, think of God [?], for such words were also spoken by Christ’s Father. Could the Father’s saying, “Where are you, Adam?” also be an expression of ignorance? This utterance is akin to that utterance. Christ asks, “Where have you laid him?” And God also asks in the Old Testament, “Where is Abel your brother?”

But perhaps someone will say, “That is not a solution to this mystery, but an addition to our doubts, for you have shown that not only Christ asks questions, but also Christ’s Father.” If that is so, let the meaning of both the Father’s and the Son’s questions also be explained. First learn the meaning of the one who asked there and of the one who asked here. But when I say “the one there” and “the one here,” I do not assign the former to one and the latter to another. Rather, I attribute what is said in the Gospel to the Father, and what is said in the Old Testament to the Son. For nothing, either in the New Testament or in the Old, happened without Christ’s power. As John also testifies, not only about creation but about the whole divine plan, “Everything came into being through him, and without him nothing came into being that came into being.” And learn the meaning of his question to Cain, “Where is Abel your brother?” By asking, he opens for him a way to give an answer. He judges as a righteous judge and calls him to repentance as one who loves humanity. “Where,” he says, “is Abel your brother?” He brings him before the tribunal as a judge. But Cain, taking the question as a sign of his ignorance, wanted to conceal the matter from his benefactor. “I do not know,” he says. “Was I my brother’s keeper?” And what follows? Consider this intention. The one who knows everything explains to him, “I deliberately pretended ignorance, but you supposed that I was asking without knowing anything. If that is so, learn the knowledge of the all-knowing one: the cry of your brother’s blood appeals to me from the earth.”

Learn now also the intention of the benefactor: what he meant when he said to the Jews, “Where have you laid him?” The assembled spectators were ungrateful, a people who could not comprehend these wonders—or rather, they did understand them, but in their ingratitude they wanted to conceal the wonders. He saw them behaving arrogantly and mocking the wonders. He looked at them as they saw his mighty works but denied the doer of good, just as David also testifies: “In the greatness of your power, your enemies have lied to you.” And what would he do about this? He could have gone there silently. Indeed, even without going there in the body, he could have sent his power, and with the rays of his power he could have broken open the tomb, raised the dead man, and brought into the light the man confined in darkness. But he wants the ungrateful themselves to be witnesses of the wonders. And before showing the tomb to the many ungrateful people, he first draws them in, saying, “Where have you laid him?” “Come,” they say, “and see the tomb.” And he says to them, “Roll away the stone.” You who became the guarantor of the disciples and gave them power as a pledge, saying, “If you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move,’ and it will move”; you who bestowed immeasurable authority on them—can you not roll away one little stone at the entrance to the tomb? But, as I said before, it was for the same reasons: they were unbelieving judges and disobedient spectators, and they would say that what happened to the dead man was some deception and trick of the eyes, and that he was pretending, listening to the misleading arrival [?]. For this reason he brings them themselves to the tomb, so that when they roll away the stone and the stench strikes their faces, the dead man’s stench may testify to them that he is truly dead. Thus, when they believe in the dead man’s death, they will no longer doubt his resurrection.

And that he devised such a means [?]—pay attention to the sequence of events there, and you will learn. Martha approached the stone and said, “Lord, he already stinks, for he has been dead four days.” But the giver of life, knowing his own power, says, “This is precisely what I want to learn from you. Say it, and keep saying that he stinks. Confirm that he is dead, so that his resurrection too may be proclaimed truthfully.” He repeated the mention of death many times, so that at least once the truth of the resurrection might also be confessed. Then, brothers, the giver of life arranges something else. He looks up to heaven and calls upon the Father. “Father,” he says, “I thank you because you have heard me.” The disciples of the heretics find a kind of remedy in these words and immediately pounce on them. “Do you see,” they say, “how great the difference is between them? One entreats, and the other is entreated; one supplicates, and the other listens to the supplications. Do you see that the Father is the source of the wonders and grants the Son the power to perform wonders?” But, as I have said many times before, they did not take it into their minds to examine the deeds of the giver of life with gratitude. Instead, having already been seized by blasphemy once and for all, they became blind and failed to discern the truth.

But learn [?] from today’s reading. The giver of life says to them, “I have shown you many good works from my Father. For which of these works do you stone me?” The Jews say to him, “We do not stone you for good works, but for blasphemy, because you are a man and make yourself God, and call God your Father.” This greatly distressed the Jews: that he called God his own Father. The Jews were angry with Christ because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his Father and made himself equal to God. And because they treated calling God his Father as blasphemy, he establishes a court at the tomb and seats truth as judge. He brings the ungrateful people around as witnesses, so that those who said, “You blaspheme because you call yourself the Son of God,” may see with their eyes and hear with their ears. He calls him Father, and by that very act he virtually instructs them: “Look, I call him this in your very presence. If he is angry because I call him Father, and if this is blasphemy, as you suppose, then let him not hear me. But if he is not angry, then it is clear that he truly is my Father.” “Father,” he says, “I thank you because you have heard me.” If the prayers were an act of obedience, how does he say, “You have heard me,” before beginning to pray? For before beginning to pray he says, “Father, I thank you because you have heard me.” And he directs the thoughts of those standing around him: “If the Father is angry,” he says, “because I call him Father, and this is some blasphemy against God, as you suppose, let him not cooperate with me, a blasphemer. But if I call the dead man and he obeys the command, receive the demonstration of the truth through the deeds themselves. For raising the dead is not the work of a blasphemer, but the command of the Son of God.” And he himself bears witness that this is the purpose of the prayers, and that he employed prayer not for any need of his own, but for the benefit and correction of his hearers. When he said, “Father, I thank you because you have heard me,” he added, “I already knew that you always hear me, but I said this because of the people standing around.”

Let no one henceforth confuse the truth; let no one oppose the worship of God; let no one count the Holy One’s coming down for our salvation as weakness or dishonor. The lover of humanity became human for your sake, not casting aside his own nature, but raising up the fallen and bringing the dead to life. He took what is yours and gives what is his. He did not come through the dispensation to his original dignity; rather, from his divinity he came to take the dispensation upon himself. It is not, as the disciples of the heretics suppose, that after the cross and the dispensation he advanced in dignity. For they wish impiously to patch certain blemishes onto the apostle’s words. When speaking of the giver of life, he says: “He who was in the form of God did not consider it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and becoming like a human being. And being found in appearance as a human being, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.” And he adds afterward: “Therefore God also highly exalted him and granted him the name that is above every name.” “Do you see,” they say, “that he received dignity as payment for his obedience? For he humbled himself to the point of death; therefore God also exalted him and granted him the name that is above every name.” If that is so, let them listen: if he received advancement as a reward for the dispensation, then he advanced from poverty to greatness. Now pay attention, I beg you: if he received advancement as a reward for obedience, then he came from poverty to greatness, to receive worship from everyone, so that every knee [?] might bend at the name of Jesus Christ. You say that he was poor and came to greatness through the dispensation. But Paul does not agree with you, for he does not show him coming from poverty to greatness, but taking poverty upon himself in his greatness.

What does the apostle say? “You know, brothers,” he says, “the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: though he was rich, he became poor for our sake, so that you might become rich through his poverty.” So that you might become rich, not so that you might blaspheme. Our Lord Jesus Christ became poor, not by casting aside his eternal riches—I mean his divinity—but by concealing them and taking this poverty upon himself. What are his riches? The Father is called rich; the Son is also called rich: rich, born of the rich. Of him Paul says that God himself enriches all who call upon him. And again: “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” Likewise, Jesus is rich, and he became poor for our sake. And in what is he rich? In being of one substance with the Father, the radiance of his glory, the imprint of his being, and the image of the invisible Father. He did not become such by acquisition, but is revealed as such by nature. Christ’s riches are these: he is equal to the Father himself and possesses the same power, glory, and kingdom; he shares the Father’s throne and has the same honor and receives the same reverence. But see into what poverty he descended, though he possessed such riches and sat above with the Father: he stood before Pilate in the courtroom like a man condemned to death. Christ’s riches are the myriads upon myriads of angels who stand in his service; Christ’s poverty is the twelve fishermen who followed him about. Christ’s riches are his throne in heaven and his sitting at the Father’s right hand; his poverty is that foxes had dens and the birds of heaven had resting places, but the Son of Man had no place to lay his head. Christ’s poverty is his riding on a young donkey, and Christ’s riches are his riding upon the cherubim. Of this the prophet says: “The chariots of God are ten thousandfold, and their drivers are thousands.” Have you seen his surpassing riches? Have you seen his poverty, filled with his saving purpose?

But perhaps [?], stirred up by heretics against the loftiness of this discourse about God, will say: “Does the statement, ‘The chariots of God are ten thousandfold,’ really refer to the Savior? Does the testimony you have brought forward really apply to him? Did it say ‘the chariots of the Son,’ or chariots honoring the Only-Begotten?” Now, so that devotion to God may not be sold away before those whose hearing is diseased, and so that the testimony may not be thought irrelevant, we must demonstrate that “The chariots of God are ten thousandfold, and their drivers are thousands” does apply to our Lord Jesus Christ. Blessed David says: “The chariots of God are ten thousandfold, and their drivers are thousands; and the Lord is among them at Sinai, in holiness. He ascended on high and took captivity captive, and gave gifts to the sons of men.” This is what David says. Let us bring forward the interpreter of the prophets, the loud-sounding trumpet, the tongue of the Holy Spirit, the one ablaze with power and every grace—Paul, the singer of the Holy One. Let us see to whom he applies the chariots of God and the words, “He ascended on high and took captivity captive, and gave gifts to the sons of men.” The apostle says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God, the Father of all, through all and in all. But to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gifts. For it says: ‘He ascended on high, took captivity captive, and gave gifts to the sons of men.’” Then, applying the meaning of the statement, Paul says: “Who is the one who ascended, if not the one who first descended into the lower regions of the earth? The one who descended is the same one who ascended into heaven, so that he might fill all things.”

There is no need for many tongues to explain, nor for many words to persuade, but for grateful minds and unity of faith, united in the confession of the Son of God. For he did not say “the unbegotten and the begotten,” nor “the uncreated and the created.” That is not unity of faith. Listen to Paul, who says, “Until we all come and attain a single unity of faith and knowledge of the Son of God.” Unity of faith is knowledge of the Son of God, not of the unbegotten and the begotten. Why do you tear out what is written? Is not the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit more trustworthy than “the unbegotten” and “the begotten,” and what is written more trustworthy than what is not written?

But the heretic objects. “Why, then,” they say, “do you speak of ‘the same essence,’ which is not written?” In the dangers of war, it is necessary to take up equipment that is not needed in peace. Who brought us into the combats of war? Was it not the hostility of the sea? And who would prepare weapons against enemies when peace abounds on every side? First put aside “a different essence,” so that “the same essence” will not confront you. But if you say “a different essence,” then “the same essence” must confront you. If you remain silent, I too will remain silent, and I recognize the [?] essence that belongs to the Father as belonging to the Son as well. For the names Father and Son have the same force, since the names Father and Son signify the same essence: the Father is the Father of the Son, and the Son is the Son of the Father, and the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God.

But see what the heretics suffer. For they were the first to provoke war, and they are ashamed to discard such thoughts. See what God's grace does in response. He saw them disobedient to God's laws and subjected them to the compulsion of Roman laws. For God [?] does the same when he sees anyone fighting against the laws of devotion to God: he raises up against them [?] of men, because they did not retain the fear of God. See what he does: anger burns in the mind of the God-fearing king, and he writes edicts concerning devotion to God through God-fearing servants, and shoots his commands like arrows from the bow of the laws.

The Savior likewise did this many times to the ungrateful Jews, who denied his devotion to God. When he spoke the truth, they would say, “By what authority do you do this?” He in turn gave an answer that could bring them to fear men: “I too will ask you one question. Where did John's baptism come from—from heaven or from men?” The Jews deliberated among themselves and said, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Then why did you not believe him?’ And if we say, ‘It was from men,’ we fear the people, lest we be stoned.” And because they had no fear of God, they set the fear of men before themselves, saying, “For fear of men, we dare not say.” And what did the Savior say in response? “Neither will I tell you. You do not even know, but I know and will not tell.”

And God stirred those thoughts, God-fearing king, for kingship is righteousness. Pay attention: kingship is also righteousness when it stands in God's service. Kingship and righteousness stand on the same level. When those who serve the kingdom do so in truth, they will share in God's honor. And listen to what Scripture says: “The souls of the righteous are in God's hands.” And what does it say about kings? “The king's heart,” it says, “is in God's hands.” And why the heart? Because the heart is the source of thoughts and the root of counsels; laws come forth from that source. For the words of kings are laws. He holds the heart in his hand so that the laws may not flow from merely human thoughts, but may come forth as though from a divine hand. The king establishes laws in agreement with God's laws. Kingship stands firmly established to exact vengeance on behalf of the heavenly kingdom—not because the kingdom above is incapable of taking vengeance on its opponents, but so that God's grace may open the door to those who are zealous for godliness.

And if we investigate carefully, we will find that whenever and wherever impiety waged war, God did not take vengeance without some righteous person. If there is no righteous man present as an intermediary, he does not take vengeance on evildoers; instead, he puts to use a human instrument filled with righteousness. Sodom and Gomorrah acted impiously, and the five cities were not destroyed until Lot had settled in the land. So that the inhabitants of the land might not say that there was no one to look to and no one's way of life to emulate, he brought the righteous man and settled him in Sodom. He lived in the same place, yet was set apart from them by his conduct. So that they might find no excuse in their defense, saying that they had no teacher, Lot appeared in Sodom, and vengeance arrived. Because they emulated neither the example nor the righteous man, they perished through fiery wrath.

Likewise, Pharaoh the Egyptian also fought against God, pleading ignorance. And the plagues did not come upon him until Moses appeared to Israel. Ahab, king of the Israelites, also acted impiously and [?] in lawless impiety. And there were no threats of wrath anywhere until Elijah the zealous appeared. Likewise, even now God can exact his own vengeance and that of this church, which is at war. But he raises up champions of godliness and wishes to care for the church through the [?] of godliness. In the same way, the blessed Elijah brought an accusation before God against Israel when he entered the wilderness, fleeing persecution by Jezebel. In response to his words, God says to him, “Why, Elijah?” God asks him, “What are you doing here?” He had gone into that wilderness where Moses received the laws, and he says, “I have been zealous with zeal for the Lord God Almighty, because the children of Israel have abandoned you. They have torn down your altars and killed your prophets. I alone remain, and they seek my life.” He says this not as though instructing God, but as one bringing an accusation; not as though informing someone who is ignorant, but as one presenting a charge to a judge: “They have torn down your altars and killed your prophets. I alone remain, and they seek my life.”

And because he was provoking him as a judge and, through his accusation, rousing him to anger as a chastiser, God wished to convince the prophet that he bears patiently with the ungodly, and that it is not through weakness that he refrains from punishing them. He says to him: “And behold, you shall go out tomorrow before me. And behold, a violent wind shall shatter the mountains and crush the hills, but the Lord shall not be in the wind. And behold, an earthquake, but the Lord shall not be in the earthquake. And behold, fire, but the Lord shall not be in the fire.” And what is the meaning of all this? “Because you think that I cannot exact vengeance, I will convince you that it is not through weakness that I refrain from bringing punishment upon the sinner. See what instruments of vengeance I have. What the sword, fire, and drowning accomplish for your judges, these accomplish for me, the great Judge. See what [?] for punishment I have: a violent wind, which can not only shatter people but also break mountains and crush hills.” And the Lord is not in the wind. This is another way of saying: “I do not wish to be known through harshness, but to be admired for gentleness.” “Behold, a violent wind,” he says, “and it shatters the mountains and crushes the hills, but the Lord is not in the wind.” “Behold, a violent wind,” he says, “and it shatters the mountains and crushes the hills, but the Lord is not in the wind.” “Behold, an earthquake”—another way of saying, “I can also destroy through an earthquake.” “And behold, fire, but the Lord is not in the fire.” He displays them, but does not put them to use.

And you yourselves bear witness to this, for he both showed an earthquake and made fire flash over the cities. He frightened them but did not punish them; he showed it and held it back. Fire flashed over the cities, the threats arrived, but his love for humanity intervened first. And, he says, one could see the people strengthened and walled about by his love for humanity. One could see everyone receiving help from great intercessors, with kingship and priesthood serving as guardians through intercession. For the God-fearing king, joined with this priesthood, interceded and appealed to God with supplications. For a righteous king can accomplish as much as the priesthood that [?], and kingship brought God to consent through intercession. Through his gentleness his glory and upright conduct were revealed. It is clear that he is the son of the great king, for that king stopped the arrows of the barbarians, while this one dispelled through prayers the arrows that rained down from the clouds.

Something like this also happened to the blessed David: God threatens him and shows his love for humanity. See what the lover of humanity does: “Here, I give you three punishments to choose from. Ask for one [?], whichever you wish: either three years of famine, or three months of war, or three days of death by pestilence.” If you are going to judge as a judge, why give him a choice? Simply punish him, for you have made justice great. He leaves the decision to him: “Whatever you wish,” he says, “I will do.” Though angry, he promises to comply. But the blessed David, bewildered by the choices, says, “I am hard pressed on every side,” and does not know what to choose: would famine be better, or war, or death? He necessarily accepts three days of death by pestilence, and not thoughtlessly, but so that the king’s devotion to God may become evident. “If I ask for famine,” he says, “I will fall under suspicion of caring nothing for the destruction of the multitude, because my kingdom has abundant provisions. And if I ask for war, I might deliver the soldiers to death while keeping myself out of danger. I will choose and ask for death, which passes over everyone alike, which shows no favoritism to the rich and no pity to the lowly, which neither honors rulers nor draws back from the poor, so that it may be evident that I have offered myself along with everyone else.”

“And the angel intervened [?],” he says, “from morning until the sixth hour, and killed seventy thousand men from among the people.” When God saw that the punishment had become severe and that there was no one to plead for mercy, since the blows were not visible, he allowed David to see the angel holding a sword in his hand and hovering in the air. David offered himself and said, “I, the shepherd, have sinned. What sin have these sheep committed? Let your hand be against me and against my father’s house.”

These words accord with those spoken in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd,” who lays down his life for his sheep. When he offered himself, he [?] God with his pleas, and God said to the angel, “Return the sword to its sheath.” Humility acted first; by falling before him, he [?] won over the great Judge. Just as the king there offered himself and dispelled the anger against everyone, so here our still more God-fearing king clothed himself in humility along with everyone, walking on foot instead of riding in chariots or on horses, and by his gentleness lessened the punishments. And because he received goodness, he repays his benefactor; because the kingdom was protected, he strengthens the church. For this very reason God said to Elijah, “Go, anoint Elisha as prophet in your place, and Jehu son of Amaziah as king over Israel, and take vengeance on the house of Ahab.” What! Is a human being to take vengeance? Rather, this was to make clear that a God-fearing kingdom avenges the truth. And that is enough on this matter.

From now on, brothers, let us flee from the harm caused by heretics and from the many waves, and bring the ship into a safe and peaceful harbor. Let us hurry, lest God’s justice arrive and sweep away sins. For example, if wood, grass, and reeds lie fallen in a field, while it is warm and clear, they do not move from their places, even though they lie scattered. But when a violent flood rises, it carries away the wood, grass, and reeds together. Likewise, when God’s judgment comes and Christ’s great tribunal is revealed, it sweeps away every error and cleanses every sin. As the prophet testifies, he says, “Judgment will surge like water, and justice will rush mightily like torrents.”

But let us bring our words to rest here and call upon the father of all, the resounding [?], the spiritual instrument. Let us call upon what is hidden and what is revealed among the treasures of the Egyptians. For it is not the church’s way to become enemies of one another, but to be a refuge for one another. Although the languages may differ, one is proclaimed in all languages. Words do not divide those whom faith does not divide; speech does not divide those whom the church’s wise teachers unite with one accord. Speak of all the practices of the church. Bless the Lord from the springs of Israel. The springs of Israel are the prophetic teachings and the law; the springs of salvation are the apostles and the gospel of salvation. Come forward, all of you, and draw water of joy from the springs of salvation.
